Mark Kellyâs (D-Ariz.) newly introduced Make AI Work for Americans Act proposes three taxes intended to capture some of the economic gains from artificial intelligence and offset the harms caused to the labor market. But the proposal exposes a fundamental gap: Congress must decide what aspect of AI activity it wants to measure before it can tax that activity coherently.

The bill puts a price on âcomputational processing,â then defines a unit of that processing as 10 kilobytes of binary data. The act would use that tax, along with levies on digital advertising and excess profits, to finance programs to help workers and communities adjust to AI-driven economic disruption.

But 10 kilobytes doesnât tell us much. A byte measures digital information, not the computational work required to produce it. And even an accurate measure of that work would still be attenuated from the billâs impetus: AI replacing human workers, depressing wages, or otherwise creating labor adjustment costs.

Lawmakers must distinguish between raising money from the AI economy and measuring the activity understood to produce harm. A given tax base neednât perfectly mirror its policy objective. But the more strained the relationship is, the more important it becomes for policymakers to explain why that specific base â and that specific taxpayer â should bear the charge.

When thereâs a direct connection between a levy and the economic harm itâs targeting, not much analytical or rhetorical work is necessary to explain the policy logic. A tax on every gallon of potable water a factory uses in production to offset the costs of that water consumption is straightforward and intuitive.

By contrast, a tax based on how many times that factory opens its front door in a day, justified to offset the cost of water use, demands much more explanation. At that point, the critical question isnât just how much is being taxed, but what opening the door has to do with water consumption.

That is the problem Kellyâs proposal raises, dressed in slightly more technical language. For example, the billâs AI usage tax doesnât measure job displacement, changes labor demands, or even computational work directly. The more disconnected the tax base is from the harm the legislation aims to address, the more important it becomes to justify why that proxy is a meaningful and fair one.

Data volume and computational work are different things. A short output may require substantial processing, while a longer one may be comparatively cheap to generate. The number of bytes in an output is a measure of data volume, not computation. But even if Congress found a much better measure of compute, it would still need to explain why more computation is a sufficiently reliable proxy for labor-market disruption or other harms.

The proposal would use one observable quantity to stand in for another and then use that second quantity to stand in for a third. That doesnât automatically make the tax incoherent, but it raises the evidentiary burden on the justification for the base. And the proposal does little to supply that justification.

The proposalâs digital advertising tax is administratively much easier to understand because it taxes something familiar and observable: 5% of covered digital advertising revenue attributable to advertisements displayed to US users. Yet that clarity also comes at the cost of a clear connection to the technology the bill is targeting.

The bill doesnât ask how much of that revenue was generated by AI, whether AI reduced labor costs in some way, or even whether the advertising displaced a single worker. It identifies a revenue stream concentrated among digital firms â cousins to AI providers, if nothing else â and taxes it.

The proposalâs excess-profits tax applies a 50% tax to the amount by which a covered taxpayerâs income exceeds 40% of gross receipts. Coverage is determined by AI-related business activity, some revenue thresholds, and substantial electricity use.

That last part gets closer to a rents theory of taxation, meaning a levy aimed at capturing exceptionally high economic returns above what would be required to induce the underlying investment. But it does nothing to isolate profits caused by AI â much less profits caused by labor displacement. A highly profitable covered firm can owe the tax without showing any excess margins were the result of displacing workers.

Conversely, a firm using AI in ways that materially reduce employment could fall outside the tax if it doesnât meet the revenue thresholds or electricity use prong. The provision basically asks: âIs this the kind of AI-related firm whose profits we feel comfortable tapping to fund the response?â And then it taxes based on the answer.

If Congress wants to tax AI directly, it first needs to define what counts as AI, determining what matters for tax purposes and developing a measurement system that bears some defensible connection to the economic effect it is trying to address. Unless those relationships are better, Congress should be cautious about dressing thin proxies up as direct taxes on AI.

A cleaner interim approach would be to simply acknowledge the uncertainty and capture some of the upside instead: taking an equity interest or otherwise making a public claim on AI company profits. That sidesteps pretending that a particular number of bytes, digital advertisement dollars, or kilowatt-hours corresponds neatly to a set number of displaced workers.

Over time, better evidence may make it possible to connect specific forms of AI use or specific model classes to measurable economic costs and then design levies to offset those costs. But until then, Congress canât measure AI harm closely enough to tax it.
